stem: In Kafka 4, a topic has two replicas and one of them has failed. A producer with `acks=all` and the default `min.insync.replicas` writes to it. What happens to the write?
key: The write succeeds, because acknowledgement needs only the in-sync replicas that remain
distractors: The write fails, because `acks=all` requires every assigned replica to acknowledge it
The write fails with `NotEnoughReplicas`, because the default `min.insync.replicas` is 2
The write succeeds only once the failed replica has caught up and rejoined the ISR
explanation: With only two replicas and one of them failed, writes that specify `acks=all` succeed. Requiring every assigned replica is wrong, because acknowledgement by all replicas does not guarantee that the full set of assigned replicas have received the message. A `NotEnoughReplicas` failure is wrong, because the default of `min.insync.replicas` is 1, not 2. Waiting for the failed replica to rejoin the ISR is wrong, because acknowledgement happens as soon as all the current in-sync replicas have received the message.
extract: then writes that specify acks=all will succeed.

stem: In Kafka, a topic's minimum ISR size is raised to a higher value for producers that use `acks=all`. Which statement describes the effect of this higher setting?
key: It trades availability for consistency: messages are written to more replicas, and writes stop when the ISR drops below the minimum
distractors: It trades consistency for availability, because fewer replicas have to acknowledge each write
It also applies to producers that use `acks=1`, so their writes wait for the minimum ISR size
It makes the producer wait for every assigned replica, including replicas outside the ISR
explanation: A higher minimum ISR size trades availability for consistency, because this setting offers a trade-off between consistency and availability. Trading consistency for availability is wrong, because a higher setting guarantees better consistency since the message is written to more replicas. Applying to `acks=1` producers is wrong, because the setting only takes effect if the producer uses `acks=all`. Waiting for every assigned replica is wrong, because acknowledgement by all replicas does not guarantee that the full set of assigned replicas have received the message.
extract: This setting offers a trade-off between consistency and availability.

stem: With the new consumer rebalance protocol of Apache Kafka 4 enabled through `group.protocol`, which of these configurations is no longer usable?
distractors: `group.consumer.assignors`
`group.remote.assignor`
`group.protocol`
explanation: `partition.assignment.strategy` is listed among the configurations and APIs that are no longer usable once the new protocol is enabled. `group.consumer.assignors` stays usable, because it specifies the list of available assignors for consumer groups. `group.remote.assignor` stays usable, because a consumer selects a different assignor through that client config. `group.protocol` stays usable, because it must be set to `consumer` to enable the new protocol.
extract: the following configurations and APIs are no longer usable

stem: Which compatibility type does the Confluent Schema Registry apply by default when a subject has no compatibility type configured?
distractors: `BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE`
`FORWARD`
`FULL`
explanation: The default compatibility type is `BACKWARD`, not `BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE`. `BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE` is wrong, because the default `BACKWARD` is non-transitive. `FORWARD` and `FULL` are wrong for one reason: BACKWARD compatibility mode is the default, and preferred for Kafka.

stem: In Kafka 4, a consumer reads from a topic, processes the records and writes results to other topics, without transactions. Which delivery guarantee does Kafka give by default?
distractors: At-most-once delivery, because the producer has retries disabled by default
Exactly-once delivery, because the consumer isolation level defaults to `read_committed`
Exactly-once delivery to any destination system, because Kafka coordinates every write with the consumer position
explanation: Kafka guarantees at-least-once delivery by default. At-most-once delivery is wrong, because the user implements it by disabling retries on the producer and committing offsets before processing. Exactly-once delivery through a `read_committed` default is wrong, because `read_uncommitted` is the default isolation level. Exactly-once delivery to any destination system is wrong, because it generally requires cooperation with such systems.
extract: Kafka guarantees at-least-once delivery by default

stem: A consumer uses `isolation.level=read_committed`, and a partition has an open transaction. Up to which offset can `consumer.poll()` return messages from that partition?
key: The last stable offset, which is one less than the offset of the first open transaction
distractors: The high watermark, because messages committed after the open transaction are already visible
Every committed message, skipping the open transaction and returning the messages that follow it
The log end offset, because the poll returns non-transactional messages out of offset order
explanation: In `read_committed` mode, `consumer.poll()` only returns messages up to the last stable offset, which is one less than the offset of the first open transaction. Reading up to the high watermark is wrong, because read-committed consumers cannot read that far while transactions are in flight. Skipping the open transaction is wrong, because messages after ongoing transactions are withheld until the transaction completes. Returning messages out of offset order is wrong, because messages are always returned in offset order.
extract: consumer.poll() will only return messages up to the last stable offset (LSO), which is the one less than the offset of the first open transaction.

stem: In Kafka 4, which producer configuration value is compatible with `enable.idempotence=true`, given that the other required settings are also respected?
distractors: `acks=1`
`retries=0`
`max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=10`
explanation: Enabling idempotence requires `acks` to be `all`. `acks=1` is wrong, because enabling idempotence requires the `acks` value to be `all`. `retries=0` is wrong, because idempotence requires `retries` to be greater than 0. A `max.in.flight.requests.per.connection` of 10 is wrong, because idempotence requires it to be less than or equal to 5.

stem: Which of these situations does NOT cause RabbitMQ to dead-letter a message, that is, to republish it to an exchange when it leaves its queue?
key: The whole queue that holds the message expires
distractors: The message expires due to its per-message TTL
A consumer rejects the message with `basic.nack` and `requeue` set to false
The message is dropped because its queue exceeded a length limit
explanation: If an entire queue expires, the messages in the queue are not dead-lettered. A message that expires due to per-message TTL is dead-lettered. A message rejected with `basic.nack` and `requeue` set to false is dead-lettered. A message dropped because its queue exceeded a length limit is dead-lettered.

stem: In Spring for Apache Kafka 4, a record keeps failing in a listener that uses the default `DefaultErrorHandler` configuration. What happens to the record once the retries are exhausted?
key: The failed record is logged at the ERROR level
distractors: The record is published to a topic named after the original topic with the `-dlt` suffix
The record is retried indefinitely until the listener succeeds
The container stops and rethrows the exception to the application
explanation: By default, after ten failures, the failed record is logged at the ERROR level. Publishing to a `-dlt` topic is wrong, because the default recoverer logs the failed record and `DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer` has to be configured to publish it. Retrying indefinitely is wrong, because it takes a `FixedBackOff` with `FixedBackOff.UNLIMITED_ATTEMPTS`. Stopping the container and rethrowing is wrong, because failures are simply logged after retries are exhausted.
